message.content:
The Battle of Waterloo (18 June 1815) was one of the bloodiest single-day engagements of the Napoleonic Wars.  While exact figures vary by source, most modern historians agree on the following rough totals:

| Side | Killed | Wounded | Missing/Prisoners | **Total Casualties** |
|------|--------|---------|-------------------|----------------------|
| French & allies (Napoleon’s army) | ~9 000–10 000 | ~12 000–13 000 | ~2 000–3 000 | **≈ 23 000–25 000** |
| Anglo‑Dutch‑Prussian coalition (Wellington’s army) | ~5 000–6 000 | ~10 000–11 000 | ~1 000–2 000 | **≈ 20 000–22 000** |

**Combined total:** roughly **43 000–47 000** casualties (killed, wounded, missing, or captured).

These numbers come from contemporary reports and later scholarly estimates.  For example, the French official report lists 9 000 killed, 12 000 wounded, and 2 000 missing, while Wellington’s own dispatches record about 5 000 killed, 10 000 wounded, and 1 000 missing.  Modern historians such as David G. Chandler and Michael Howard cite similar figures, noting that battlefield conditions, record‑keeping practices, and post‑battle attrition can cause variations of a few thousand.
